tier_reason: The cited Turbo-Base64 table is only tier C: its third-party harness (xtb64.mak, xb64test.h, xtb64test_.c) is not in the public repo, and it gives no flags beyond 'gcc 11.2'. Stronger evidence exists and keeps tier A: Muła & Lemire, 'Faster Base64 Encoding and Decoding Using AVX2 Instructions' (ACM TWEB 2018, arXiv 1704.00605), Table VI benchmarks aklomp's AVX2 decoder against Chrome and Linux base64 on an i7-6700 with GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native. Its public artifact is lemire/fastbase64: benchmarks/basic_benchmark.c, src/klompavxbase64.c and a Makefile with -O3 -march=native -mavx2.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Muła & Lemire (ACM TWEB 2018) Table VI, decode on real files: AVX2 (Klomp) 0.43 cycles/byte vs Google Chrome base64 1.8 and Linux kernel base64 20 on lena.jpg (~4.2x vs Chrome, ~46x vs Linux, derived from page data). Also Turbo-Base64 README (1 MB buffer, i7-9700K, gcc 11.2): b64avx2 26,153 MB/s encode / 22,515 MB/s decode vs Google Chrome base64 2,541/4,289 MB/s (~10x encode, ~5x decode, derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Single-threaded base64 decode of real files (images, text, 1.4-330 KB) with error checking, from the Muła & Lemire paper; plus encode/decode of a 1 MB buffer from the Turbo-Base64 README shootout
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native (Muła & Lemire paper, lemire/fastbase64 Makefile adds -mavx2). The Turbo-Base64 table states only gcc 11.2, with no flags given for the competitor builds
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, Turbo Boost disabled (paper); Intel i7-9700K @ 3.6 GHz (Turbo-Base64 table)
corrections.caveats: The paper benchmarks a 2017 copy of aklomp's AVX2 decoder vendored into lemire/fastbase64 ('based on Alfred Klomp's code with minor modifications'), decode only. The paper's own AVX2 codec is about 2x faster than Klomp's. The Turbo-Base64 numbers come from a competitor's 2022.02 run against aklomp v2022.02, and its comparison harness is not public. The latest commit (2026-07) only touches CI; the last code change was 2025-05.

notes: Tier A holds, but through the peer-reviewed paper and its artifact repo, not through the cited Turbo-Base64 page, which alone would be tier C. benchmark_url was switched to the paper. Metadata checks out: BSD-2-Clause, 1,022 stars, not archived or a fork.

tier_reason: These are first-party numbers. The public benchmark (benches/benchmark.rs, Criterion) measures only crc-fast and never runs the `crc` crate baseline. The '~0.5GiB/s' baseline and 'up to >220X' are a one-line README assertion with no hardware stated, and the link points to an anchor that no longer exists. The rustc version is not stated either, and a >50x gain with unstated flags is capped at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README asserts the `crc` crate is ~0.5 GiB/s by default, so crc-fast is 'up to >220X faster'; baseline is unbenchmarked. README table: CRC-32/ISCSI ~111 GiB/s at 1 MiB (~61 GiB/s at 1 KiB) on Sapphire Rapids EC2 c7i.metal-24xl, avx512-vpclmulqdq. 111 vs 0.5 GiB/s is ~222x (derived from page data)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc version not stated (MSRV 1.89); Cargo release profile lto = true; runtime-dispatched target feature listed per row (e.g. avx512-vpclmulqdq, neon-pmull-sha3)
corrections.caveats: The baseline `crc` crate (~0.5 GiB/s default) is never benchmarked side by side, with no hardware given for it. It is also a weak baseline: crc32fast, the common Rust CRC-32 incumbent, already uses PCLMULQDQ. Numbers are first-party and the rustc version is unstated. The C/C++ interface is an FFI shared/static library plus a generated header (libcrc_fast.h).

notes: This is a real, widely downloaded crate, but the evidence for the >220x claim is only an unmeasured baseline figure. The last commit (2025-12-27) is within 12 months, so it counts as active, not stale. GitHub detects only Apache-2.0, but Cargo.toml and the README give dual MIT OR Apache-2.0.

tier_reason: The README benchmarks the new kernels head to head against Chromium's zlib crc32.c and crc32_simd.c, which are vendored in third_party/, plus dougallj's and corsix's earlier crc32c_4k code. It gives exact reproduce commands for bench.c and autobench.c, the Makefile and third_party/Makefile build everything with gcc -O3 -march=native, and each CPU is identified by a /proc/cpuinfo dump. The only gap is that the compiler version is not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline vs previous state of the art: Apple M1 9.6% faster (77.55->85.05 GB/s; baseline dougallj Faster CRC32); Cascade Lake 25% (25.32->31.55 GB/s; baseline corsix crc32_4k_fusion); Ice Lake 56% (41.00->63.98 GB/s; baseline Chromium zlib vector AVX512 CRC32); Sapphire Rapids 19% (81.68->97.30 GB/s; baseline Chromium zlib vector AVX512, aligned inputs). Against Chromium zlib's NEON vector CRC32 on M1: 26.57->85.05 GB/s (~3.2x, derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Single-core CRC32/CRC32C throughput on large buffers across x86_64 (SSE, AVX-512, AVX-512+VPCLMULQDQ) and aarch64 (NEON, NEON+EOR3). Compared against Chromium zlib's crc32.c/crc32_simd.c, dougallj's Faster CRC32 (M1, Ampere Altra) and the author's earlier crc32_4k_* implementations
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc (version not stated) -O3 -march=native for the generated kernels (Makefile) and the Chromium/dougallj baselines (third_party/Makefile); per-ISA gcc-equivalent flags documented, e.g. -msse4.2 -mpclmul, -mavx512f -mavx512vl -mvpclmulqdq, -march=armv8-a+crypto+crc
corrections.hardware: Apple M1; GCP Tau T2A (Ampere Altra); Intel Xeon Silver 4214 @2.2GHz (Cascade Lake), Intel Xeon @2.6GHz (Ice Lake), Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C @2.7GHz (Sapphire Rapids); AMD EPYC 7B12 (Rome/Zen2), EPYC 7B13 (Milan/Zen3), EPYC 9B14 (Genoa/Zen4) (/proc/cpuinfo excerpts in README)
corrections.caveats: Baselines are prior state-of-the-art SIMD code (Chromium zlib vectorized CRC32, dougallj, the author's crc32_4k), not naive table-driven CRC32. On Ice Lake and Sapphire Rapids the headline pits Chromium's CRC32 (zlib polynomial) against the new CRC32C kernel. The Sapphire Rapids baseline uses Chromium with aligned inputs; unaligned it is 65.20 GB/s. The repo is a code generator plus sample outputs, not a packaged library.

notes: Tier A is confirmed. The last commit (2025-11-27) is within 12 months, so it counts as active, not stale. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but LICENSE.md offers a choice of MIT or zlib, so 'MIT OR Zlib' is correct.
